title: Geometry-controlled correlated electric-field noise in enclosed ion traps from billiard return spectra
abstract: We ask how passive conducting geometry determines the spatial structure of electric-field noise seen by trapped ions. From a boundary-potential covariance and the Dirichlet Green function we construct the $N$-ion electric-field cross-spectral matrix and its blockwise motional Kossakowski generator. In a parallel slab, billiard unfolding turns the electrostatic response into a return-depth measure and yields an exact return-pair functional for arbitrary stationary surface spectra. For every finite equal-height ion array, the passive cover increases the normal-field covariance matrix in the positive-semidefinite ordering and decreases the tangential-field covariance matrix in the same ordering: all collective normal-field coordinates acquire more absolute noise, while all collective tangential coordinates acquire less. At $h=2d$ the local-noise single-ion ratios are exactly $ζ(3)$ and $η(3)$.   Diagonalizing the equal-frequency covariance identifies collective environmental noise eigenchannels and a geometry-dependent noise rank; within a degenerate frequency block these become the Lindblad jump channels. In a ten-ion example, closing the cover to $h=2d$ lowers the participation rank from 5.61 to 5.11 while increasing the leading channel's share from 23.7% to 28.6%; a primitive Mølmer-Sørensen calculation shows how the projected covariance sets the weak-heating gate exposure. Beyond parallel walls, specular paths emerge as large-$q_z$ saddles of the screened boundary operator. Across 16 curved covers, the fitted electrostatic decay exponent correlates at 0.9991 with the independently computed shortest specular excess length, while separate tests resolve focusing and competing saddles.
summary: This theoretical paper determines how the physical boundaries of an ion trap control the correlated electric-field noise acting on trapped ions. By employing techniques from spectral theory and billiards, the authors show that the enclosure geometry selectively enhances normal-field noise while suppressing tangential-field noise. This provides a fundamental understanding of how passive electrode design can be used to engineer the quantum noise environment for quantum computing applications.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the passive conducting geometry of an enclosed ion trap dictates the spatial structure and magnitude of correlated electric-field noise experienced by trapped ions.
main_result: The enclosure geometry imposes a mode-selective filtering effect, increasing normal-field noise while decreasing tangential-field noise, and provides an exact return-pair functional describing this noise.
method: The analysis uses boundary-potential covariance, the Dirichlet Green function, and billiard unfolding techniques to construct the electric-field cross-spectral matrix and its associated Kossakowski generator.
model_or_system: The system is trapped ions confined within an enclosed geometry, such as a parallel slab or a general curved cover. The noise source is modeled as a stochastic electric field fluctuating due to the surrounding passive conductors.
key_observables: Electric-field cross-spectral matrix, collective environmental noise eigenchannels, noise rank, and the ratio of normal-to-tangential heating rates ($\zeta(3)$ and $\eta(3)$ at specific limits).
important_parameters: The ratio of cover height to ion spacing ($h/d$), the frequency ($\omega$), and the ion number ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Born–Markov secular approximation and assumes fixed stochastic source statistics, focusing on the geometric reshaping of the noise operator.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mode-selective filtering effect (normal vs. tangential heating ratios) and show the correlation between the electrostatic decay exponent and the shortest specular excess length across curved covers.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general framework using boundary-potential covariance to deriving the exact return-pair functional for the parallel slab. It then applies this framework to show the collective ordering theorem for normal/tangential fields and extends the analysis to general curved covers, concluding with diagnostics on noise rank and gate exposure.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, quantitative link between macroscopic electrostatics (geometry) and microscopic quantum noise processes (heating rates, Lindblad operators) in trapped ions, offering a new diagnostic tool for trap quality.
